title: Statistical Language Competition Model with Dynamic Edge Weighting on a Random Network
authors: Somyaranjan Chakra, Mohit Anand Madhesia, Shradha Mishra
abstract: This paper presents a computational study of language competition dynamics on Erdős--Rényi random networks, extending the foundational Abrams--Strogatz model through two novel contributions: (i) a dynamic edge-weighting mechanism that reinforces social ties between co-minority speakers by an additive increment $Δ$, and (ii) a probabilistic agent-based framework governing language switching via a weighted majority rule. Phase boundaries separating the dominance and coexistence regimes are identified across a two-dimensional parameter space $(p, Δ)$, where $p$ denotes the network connectivity probability. We further characterise anomalous persistence zones within predicted dominance regions, attributing them to the formation of isolated minority speaker clusters. Scaling study across network sizes $N \in \{50, 100, 250, 500, 1000\}$ reveal that average cluster size decreases with $N$ and that phase boundaries diffuse with increasing stochastic noise. Finally, we discuss extensions to a tripartite bilingual model and heterogeneous prestige/volatility to more faithfully capture real sociolinguistic contact scenarios.
summary: This paper models language competition on random networks, extending classical models by incorporating dynamic social reinforcement between minority speakers. It maps out the parameter space where minority languages can persist against majority pressure, showing that network structure and local reinforcement are key competing factors. The work also extends the model to include bilingualism, demonstrating its role in stabilizing coexistence regimes.
main_problem: The paper investigates language competition dynamics, modeling how minority language speakers reinforce local social ties to resist assimilation pressure from a majority language.
main_result: The interplay between network connectivity ($p$) and adaptive edge reinforcement ($\Delta$) determines the phase boundary between language dominance and coexistence regimes. Furthermore, the inclusion of bilingual speakers enriches dynamics by promoting coexistence.
method: The study uses agent-based simulations on Erdős–Rényi random networks, employing a weighted majority rule for language switching and Support Vector Machines (SVM) for formal phase boundary identification.
model_or_system: The system is a set of agents on a random network where language switching is governed by weighted local influence. The model extends the Abrams–Strogatz framework with a dynamic edge-weighting mechanism that reinforces ties between co-minority speakers.
key_observables: Final majority-language density ($ho$), average minority cluster size, phase boundary location in $(p, \Delta)$ space, and anomaly density.
important_parameters: Network connectivity probability ($p$), reinforcement strength ($\Delta$), language prestige ($s$), and network size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The initial state assumes equal language densities ($ho_A(0) = ho_B(0) = 0.5$), and the analysis notes limitations regarding fixed simulation time steps ($T$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase boundaries and anomalous cluster formations across varying network sizes ($N$) and simulation times ($T$), showing how these boundaries shift and sharpen with increased time.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the foundational Abrams–Strogatz model by introducing dynamic edge weighting and a probabilistic agent-based framework. It analyzes phase boundaries in $(p, \Delta)$ space, characterizes anomalous persistence zones, and extends the model to include bilingual speakers in a tripartite state space.
why_interesting: While focused on sociolinguistics, the underlying mathematical framework—modeling phase transitions, critical points, and non-equilibrium dynamics on complex networks—is directly analogous to many physical systems studied in statistical mechanics, such as pattern formation or phase transitions in interacting particle systems.

Fig.1 provides a schematic illustration of the probabilis- tic agent-based framework employed in this study. The central node i interacts with its neighbouring agents through weighted edges, where each edge weight rep- resents the strength of social interaction between two connected individuals. The neighbouring nodes belong to either Language A or Language B, and the weighted contributions from each language are accumulated sepa- rately to determine the local linguistic influence on the central node [8].
